name: Whering
tagline: A digital wardrobe app: photograph your clothes, cut them out, build outfits, track what you actually wear.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The hard part of a wardrobe app used to be cutting garments out of photos, and that is now a library call that runs on your laptop. An agent can give you a local catalog with photos, tags, a drag-and-drop outfit canvas, a wear calendar and cost-per-wear math in a weekend. What it cannot give you cheaply is the phone-shaped part: a camera-first capture flow you will actually use while standing in front of a closet, plus sync between your phone and wherever the data lives. Also gone is the auto-tagging that guesses brand, colour and category from a photo, the resale and shopping integrations, and other people's outfits to steal ideas from. If you are disciplined enough to bulk-upload once from a desktop, the DIY version is genuinely fine; if you are not, you will stop using it in nine days.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app where you upload garment photos, get the background removed automatically, tag and search the items, drag them onto an outfit canvas, and log what you wore to see wear counts and cost per wear.
requirements: Node 20+ and a machine with a few GB of RAM for the local background-removal model
Your own garment photos, shot against a plain-ish background
Willingness to use it as a PWA on your phone rather than a native app
whatYouLose: Native iOS/Android app with a tuned camera capture flow
Automatic garment recognition: category, colour and brand guessed from the photo
Cloud sync and backup across devices
Resale, shopping and brand integrations, plus the community outfit feed
Weather-aware and occasion-based outfit suggestions that are actually tuned
moatNotes: The auto-tagging model is trained on a large pile of user-uploaded garments, which is not something you bootstrap alone.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because wardrobe apps live or die on capture friction, and that is an interface problem, not a logic problem. Whering has spent years making the photograph, cut out, tag, done loop fast enough that people get through fifty items in a sitting, and it auto-guesses most of the metadata so you are confirming rather than typing. A personal build gets you the same database and the same outfit canvas, but you are the auto-tagger, and the honest failure mode of DIY wardrobe software is a half-populated catalog that you abandon.
notes: The background-removal step stopped being impressive about two years ago; the capture habit is still the whole game.
prompt:
Build a local-first digital wardrobe app called Closet. Stack: Next.js 15 (App Router, TypeScript), SQLite via better-sqlite3, Tailwind for styling, dnd-kit for drag and drop. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry, no external APIs. Everything runs on localhost and stores data on disk.

Data model (SQLite, migrations in /db/migrations, run on boot):
- items: id, name, category (top, bottom, outerwear, dress, shoes, bag, accessory), colour, brand, price_paid, season (array as JSON), notes, image_path, cutout_path, archived, created_at
- outfits: id, name, occasion, canvas_json (positions, scale, z-index per item), thumbnail_path, created_at
- outfit_items: outfit_id, item_id
- wears: id, date, outfit_id nullable, item_id nullable (log either an outfit or a single item)

Features, in scope:
1. Upload page: drop one or many photos. For each, run background removal locally with @imgly/background-removal-node and save both the original and a transparent PNG cutout into /data/images. Show a grid of results and let me edit name, category, colour, brand and price inline before saving.
2. Wardrobe grid: filter by category, colour, season, brand; search by name; toggle archived. Show the cutout on a neutral background.
3. Outfit builder: a canvas where I drag items from a sidebar, move, scale and layer them. Save the layout to canvas_json and render a thumbnail by compositing the cutouts with sharp.
4. Wear log: a month calendar. Click a day, pick an outfit or individual items, save. Each item page shows wear count, last worn, and cost per wear (price_paid divided by wear count).
5. Stats page: most and least worn items, items never worn after 60 days, total wardrobe value, spend per category.

Out of scope, do not build: auto-tagging from images, weather suggestions, social feeds, resale links, multi-user anything, auth.

Make it mobile-usable: add a web app manifest and make the upload page accept camera capture on phones, so I can add it to my home screen and hit it over the LAN. Put the SQLite path and image directory in .env with sane defaults. Seed nothing. Write a README with setup, the dev command, and one paragraph on how to back up /data by copying the folder.
